prompt: A fintech company runs a payment event pipeline. A consumer application that runs on an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group (8 instances) reads from an Amazon Kinesis Data Streams stream (24-hour retention period, 12 shards). Right after a deployment last month, consumer processing fell behind, and no one noticed until some records were about to expire. Verifying data consistency afterward took two days. The current Amazon CloudWatch dashboard shows only EC2 CPU utilization. The company wants to use a metric that shows how far the consumer has fallen behind the end of the stream to raise an alarm in advance about the risk of data loss caused by retention period expiration. The consumer code must not be modified, and notifications must be sent to an existing Amazon SNS topic. Which CloudWatch alarm is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Raise an alarm when the Sum of IncomingBytes exceeds the number of shards multiplied by 1 MB/s, the per-shard write limit.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Raise an alarm when the Maximum statistic of GetRecords.IteratorAgeMilliseconds exceeds 12 hours, which is 50% of the retention period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Raise an alarm, treating the consumer as lagging, when the Minimum statistic of ReadProvisionedThroughputExceeded is 0.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Raise an alarm when the Maximum statistic of GetRecords.Success is not 1, on the assumption that the consumer is reading normally when the value is 1.

explanation: The correct answer is to set an alarm on the Maximum of GetRecords.IteratorAgeMilliseconds. This metric is the age of the last record read by GetRecords calls, and a value of 0 means the consumer has caught up with the end of the stream. The official documentation states that when the value exceeds 50% of the retention period, there is a risk of losing data because records expire, and it recommends setting an alarm on the Maximum statistic. IncomingBytes reflects producer-side write volume and is unrelated to consumer lag. A Minimum of 0 for the read throttling metric does not indicate whether the consumer is lagging. GetRecords.Success is the count of successful calls, and a maximum-of-1 criterion does not describe lag.

prompt: A SaaS company keeps application log indexes for 90 days in an Amazon OpenSearch Service domain (6 data nodes, high-performance EBS storage). Indexes are created daily. Indexes older than 7 days no longer receive writes, and the support team occasionally searches them when investigating incidents. Slightly higher search latency is acceptable, but data within the 90 days must not be deleted. Storage costs are exceeding the monthly budget, so the company wants to move old indexes to a cheaper tier without deleting them, and does not want anyone to have to move indexes manually every day. The domain currently uses dedicated master nodes. The index retention policy was agreed with the audit team last quarter, so the 90 days cannot be shortened. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Migrate indexes older than 7 days to the UltraWarm tier and automate the migration with an Index State Management (ISM) policy. Warm indexes are backed by Amazon S3 and become read-only.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Replace the data nodes with larger instances and reduce the number of replicas of old indexes to 0 to cut EBS usage, but keep all indexes in the hot tier. Shard data can be lost if a node fails.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Manually delete indexes older than 7 days every day, and operate a procedure to restore the index from a snapshot as a new index whenever a search is needed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Keep adding new documents to indexes older than 7 days while moving them to the warm tier, and configure the warm tier so that indexing performance stays the same as the hot tier.

explanation: The correct answer is to migrate to UltraWarm and automate it with ISM. UltraWarm uses Amazon S3 and a cache instead of EBS to store indexes that are no longer written to at a much lower price per GiB, and they can still be searched with the same APIs. Replicas are not needed, so storage is counted only for the primary shard size. Replacing nodes with larger ones actually increases cost, and removing replicas reduces availability in the hot tier. Manual deletion and snapshot restores harm searchability and impose a heavy operational burden. Warm indexes are read-only, so the premise of continuing to add documents does not hold.

prompt: A retail company has an Amazon Redshift cluster with a WLM queue that has concurrency scaling turned on. During month-end reporting hours, some queries keep waiting in the queue on the main cluster. The queue is already configured with auto WLM, and the concurrency scaling mode is also auto. The monthly free credits have not been used up, so the cost limit is not the cause, and query wait times remain long. An investigation shows that the queries remaining in the queue have something in common. The analytics team is pulling query results into a BI tool and does not plan to change the number of nodes in the cluster. Which TWO are causes of these queries not being routed to the concurrency scaling cluster? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: The query returns fewer than 1,000 result rows.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The query reads a temporary table.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The query reads a table that uses an interleaved sort key.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The query is a SELECT that reads a table distributed with DISTSTYLE KEY.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The query is a SELECT that reads a regular table that uses a compound sort key.

explanation: The correct answers are queries on tables with interleaved sort keys and queries on temporary tables. The limitations in the official documentation state that concurrency scaling does not support queries on tables that use interleaved sort keys or queries on temporary tables. Compound sort keys are not on the list of limitations. The number of result rows is not a routing criterion. Reading a DISTSTYLE KEY table is not a limitation either, and DISTSTYLE ALL is a problem only for write operations on the target table.

prompt: A logistics company has an AWS Glue ETL job that incrementally processes Amazon S3 input by using job bookmarks and writes Parquet output to an output path every morning. A bug in the transformation logic was found in the last 3 runs, and incorrect amounts flowed into an aggregate table. Only the input for those 3 runs must be reprocessed. The input bucket holds 2 years of history, and reading all of it again is unacceptable in terms of time and cost. The reprocessed results also must not be mixed with the existing incorrect output and create duplicates. The fixed script has already been deployed, and two data engineers must finish the recovery today. Input files are separated by daily prefixes, and the source files for the last 3 days all remain intact. What should the company do?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Rewind the bookmark to the point of the last good run before the bug, and rerun the job, but first delete the incorrect output of the 3 runs or write the new output to a separate output location.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reset the bookmark, run the job once to reprocess all 2 years of input, and overwrite all files in the output path (leave the script as it is).

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rerun the job with the bookmark disabled on the same input path, and AWS Glue will track the previous output files and automatically replace the incorrect results.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Delete the job and recreate it with the same name to start with a fresh bookmark state, and expect it to read only the input of the 3 runs.

explanation: The correct answer is to rewind the bookmark to the point of a good run and rerun, while cleaning up the incorrect output or writing it to a different location. Rewinding causes only the source files from subsequent runs to be reprocessed, so only the 3 runs are read. However, bookmarks track only source files and do not delete target files, so the output must be cleaned up. A reset would cause the entire history to be read again, which violates the cost constraint. Disabling the bookmark always processes the entire dataset, and managing previous output is the user's responsibility, so no automatic replacement occurs. Deleting the job also deletes the bookmarks stored per job, which has the same result as a reset and reads everything again.

prompt: At a media company, an AWS Glue job normally finishes in 20 minutes under the SLA, but when input surges it runs for several hours and eventually succeeds. This delay blocks the distribution of downstream reports, but the job neither fails nor times out, so no alert is currently sent. The company wants to be notified through Amazon SNS immediately if the job is running for more than 45 minutes, without waiting for it to finish. The job runs once a day in the early morning, and no Amazon EventBridge rule has been created yet. The operations team has three people, the job code must not be changed, and the job must not be forcibly terminated. The team that owns the job wants the on-call engineer on weekday mornings to receive this alert on a mobile phone through an SMS subscription to the SNS topic. Which is the simplest way to meet these requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Set the job delay notification threshold of the job to 45 minutes, and create an EventBridge rule that matches Glue Job Run Status events and sends them to the SNS topic.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create a rule that matches the SUCCEEDED state of Glue Job State Change events, and have an AWS Lambda function that receives the event calculate the difference between the start and end times and send an SNS notification if it exceeds 45 minutes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lower the job Timeout value to 45 minutes so that runs exceeding 45 minutes end in the TIMEOUT state, and receive notifications through an EventBridge rule that matches that state change event and sends it to SNS.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Run a separate AWS Step Functions state machine each time the job starts, with a 45-minute wait state, and when the wait ends, call GetJobRun to check the job state and send an SNS notification if it is RUNNING.

explanation: The correct answer is to set the delay notification threshold and use Glue Job Run Status events. According to the documentation, when a run in the STARTING, RUNNING, or STOPPING state exceeds the job delay notification threshold, a Glue Job Run Status event is generated once, so a notification can be received while the job is still running, without code changes. Calculating from the success event means finding out only after the job has finished, which is not an immediate notification. Lowering the Timeout would forcibly terminate the job instead of sending a notification, causing a job that used to eventually succeed to fail. Running Step Functions separately requires building orchestration for each job, which is not simple.

prompt: At an insurance company, an AWS Lambda function writes the transformed result of each raw CSV file uploaded to Amazon S3 to a curated prefix in the same bucket. About 40,000 files are uploaded per day, and the Lambda function finishes within a few seconds per file. S3 event notifications can occasionally deliver the same event twice, and Lambda can also be retried on errors. Even if the same source is processed twice, no duplicate files may be created in curated, and the company does not want a separate state store such as Amazon DynamoDB. With a small operations staff, the company also wants to avoid adding components. The curated results are read once a day by an AWS Glue crawler, and one source file always corresponds to one result file. What is the simplest design?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Allow duplicate files in curated, and use SELECT DISTINCT in Amazon Athena queries to remove duplicate rows every time the data is read.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Change the target of the S3 event notification directly to an Amazon SQS FIFO queue so that the message deduplication feature ensures the same event is processed only once.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Append a processing timestamp to the output object key so that each run creates a unique file, and later delete old files with a lifecycle rule.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Derive the output object key deterministically from the source object key (and version ID) so that if the same source is processed again, it overwrites the same key.

explanation: The correct answer is a design that derives the output key deterministically from the source key. Even if the same event is processed twice, the same content is overwritten at the same key, so the operation is idempotent and no separate state store is needed. S3 event notifications are delivered at least once and can occasionally be duplicated. A timestamped key creates a new file each time it is processed, which actually creates duplicates. S3 event notifications do not directly support an SQS FIFO queue as a destination. Removing duplicates with DISTINCT at read time leaves the duplicate files in place and only increases query cost and scan volume.

prompt: A security company has accumulated about 300 million log objects of around 10 KB each in Amazon S3, which must be retained for 7 years because of regulations. They are accessed less than once a year, and it is acceptable if restoring them takes several hours during an audit. All of them are currently in S3 Standard, and the company plans to use a lifecycle rule to transition each object directly to S3 Glacier Deep Archive. The cost owner is concerned that, because there are so many objects, the transition request charges and the additional per-object metadata storage will reduce the savings. Logs are generated daily, and the ingestion pipeline can be modified. The transition requests created by the current lifecycle rule are noticeably large on the monthly bill, and the finance team is asking why. Which method reduces cost MOST efficiently while meeting the retention requirement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Keep the Deep Archive transition rule as it is, and add a rule that limits the number of objects transitioned per day to reduce transition request charges.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Leave the objects in S3 Standard and set only a rule that deletes them after 7 years, which eliminates both the transition request charges and the metadata charges.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Combine the small log objects into larger objects, such as daily compressed bundles or Parquet files, then transition the combined objects to Deep Archive and delete them after 7 years.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Store the objects in S3 Intelligent-Tiering and enable the Deep Archive Access tier so that even small objects are automatically placed in the cheapest tier.

explanation: The correct answer is to combine small objects into larger objects and transition them to Deep Archive. A transition request charge applies once for each object transitioned to the Glacier classes, and S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval and Deep Archive add about 40 KB of metadata storage per object (8 KB billed at the Standard rate and 32 KB at the archive rate). The official documentation also advises aggregating small objects into larger ones. Limiting the number of objects transitioned per day does not reduce cost; it only delays the transition. Keeping data in Standard for 7 years means continuing to pay the most expensive rate for data accessed less than once a year. Intelligent-Tiering does not treat objects smaller than 128 KB as eligible for automatic tiering, so 10 KB objects would see almost no savings.

prompt: An advertising analytics company stores event data in Amazon S3 partitioned as region=<region code>/dt=<date> and queries it with Amazon Athena. There are hundreds of candidate region codes and the date range spans several years, but combinations that actually contain data are less than 10% of all combinations, and only a few regions are loaded every day. Partitions are currently registered with an AWS Glue crawler, and the operations team believes that switching to partition projection would let them eliminate the crawler and wants to try it. However, the Athena official documentation explains that Athena projects partitions that do not exist without error but may be slower than regular AWS Glue partitions if many partitions are empty, and recommends regular partitions if more than half of the projected partitions are empty. This table far exceeds that threshold. Loading is performed by an AWS Glue job, and the loading code can be modified. The data engineering team has been given a goal of reducing crawler cost within the quarter, but cannot sacrifice query response time. Which partition management approach is MOST appropriate for this situation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Use a projection as is, with the entire set of region code candidates as a value list and the entire multi-year date range as the date range, and leave it to Athena to treat nonexistent combinations as empty results.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Delete the region code partition key and configure only the date partition with projection, and filter by region only with a WHERE clause in queries.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Turn on both projection and regular partition registration for the same table so that Athena combines the partition information from both methods.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Do not use projection. Continue with the existing approach of registering only the partitions that actually exist in the AWS Glue Data Catalog, and add new partitions by using the partition registration API when loading finishes.

explanation: The correct answer is the existing approach of registering only the partitions that actually exist. The documentation explains that Athena projects nonexistent projected partitions and returns empty results without error, but that it can be slower than regular AWS Glue partitions when many partitions are empty, and that regular partitions are recommended when more than half are empty. This table has actual combinations of less than 10%, so more than 90% are empty, which falls under that recommendation. Projecting all values broadly would create exactly that problem. Removing the region key would increase scan volume and cost. Also, when projection is enabled, Athena ignores the partition metadata registered in the catalog, so merging the two approaches does not work.

prompt: At a financial company ahead of a year-end audit, the compliance team requires that the metadata of databases, tables, and partitions stored in the AWS Glue Data Catalog be encrypted with a customer managed key. Hundreds of tables are registered in the catalog and are accessed by several analyst roles and AWS Glue ETL job roles, and existing ETL job code must not be changed. The Amazon S3 buckets that store the data are already encrypted with SSE-KMS, and job output is also encrypted through a separate setting. Keys are managed in a single account and no external key store is used. The audit is 4 weeks away, and a large-scale migration that recreates the catalog objects has not been approved. Which action is MOST appropriate to meet the catalog metadata encryption requirement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Turn on metadata encryption in the Data Catalog settings, specify a symmetric customer managed key, and grant key permissions to the principals that access the catalog.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create an AWS Glue security configuration and attach it to all jobs and crawlers so that metadata stored in the catalog is also encrypted with the same key.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create a new asymmetric AWS KMS key and specify it as the catalog encryption key so that metadata is protected with a key that can sign and verify.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Set the default encryption of the S3 buckets that the catalog points to as SSE-KMS and treat the catalog metadata as also encrypted.

explanation: The correct answer is to turn on metadata encryption in the Data Catalog settings and specify a symmetric customer managed key. Once enabled, objects created afterward, such as databases, tables, and partitions, are encrypted with the KMS key. Principals that access them need key usage permissions such as Decrypt, and no job code changes. A security configuration is for job output (Amazon S3), Amazon CloudWatch logs, and bookmark encryption, and does not cover catalog metadata. S3 bucket encryption applies only to data objects. AWS Glue supports only symmetric customer managed keys, so an asymmetric key cannot be used.

prompt: An advertising company has accumulated several years of logs in Amazon S3, partitioned by hourly date (dt) and region code (region, 10 values), with hundreds of thousands of partitions. Most Amazon Athena queries read only the most recent day, but fetching partition metadata before a query starts takes a long time, so dashboard responses are slow. The company also wants to reduce the operation of the crawler that registers new hourly partitions. Partition values are regular, based on a date range and a fixed list of regions, and the S3 path convention will not change. The company wants a solution that does not increase scan costs and does not place a new component in front of the queries. The BI tool runs the same query hundreds of times a day, so the delay in starting queries directly affects the user experience. Which is the MOST appropriate method?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Change the AWS Glue crawler schedule to run every 5 minutes so that new partitions are registered in the catalog as soon as they are created, and leave the queries as they are.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Remove all partition keys, place all logs in a single path, and filter by date with a WHERE clause in each query to eliminate the metadata lookup.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Configure Athena partition projection as table properties so that Athena computes the date range and region values directly, and stops looking up partitions in the catalog.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Place an AWS Lambda function in front of queries that registers only the needed partitions with ALTER TABLE ADD PARTITION just before the query, and have the BI tool call this function first.

explanation: The correct answer is partition projection. Projection computes partition locations in memory from the ranges and value lists in table properties, so the AWS Glue catalog GetPartitions call is not needed and the separate work of registering new partitions disappears. A date range and a fixed region list are the regular structure that is easiest to configure for projection. Shortening the crawler interval makes registration faster, but the metadata lookup delay before queries remains and only crawler cost increases. Removing partitions makes every query scan everything, causing scan volume and cost to explode. A Lambda function in front of queries adds a new component and latency, and does not solve the problem of metadata for hundreds of thousands of partitions.

prompt: At an e-commerce company's Amazon Redshift RA3 cluster (8 nodes), every day for 30 minutes around 9 AM, simultaneous BI dashboard access by hundreds of sales representatives causes queries to wait in the queue for a long time. Capacity is sufficient the rest of the time, and the overnight ETL runs without problems in a separate queue. The company wants to avoid permanently enlarging the cluster because of cost, and wants to use additional capacity only when access surges, without creating new manual operations or building a custom scheduler. The dashboard is interactive and runs queries on demand whenever a user changes a filter. Most dashboard queries are short lookups that finish within a few seconds, and the number of users stays about the same at month-end. Which is the MOST cost-effective method?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Permanently scale the cluster out to 16 RA3 nodes so that capacity is always available to prevent queueing even during the hours when access surges.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In the WLM queue to which dashboard queries are assigned, set the concurrency scaling mode to auto so that additional clusters process eligible queries when waits occur.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Use elastic resize to add nodes at 8 AM and remove them at 10 AM on a schedule built with AWS Lambda and Amazon EventBridge that runs automatically every day.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Export all query results shown by the dashboard to CSV every day and store them in Amazon S3, and have the BI tool read those files to eliminate queries on the cluster.

explanation: The correct answer is to turn on concurrency scaling in the WLM queue. When the queue mode is auto, eligible queries that exceed the queue concurrency are sent to additional clusters instead of waiting, and charges apply only for the time those clusters actually process queries. Permanently expanding to 16 nodes means continuously paying for capacity that would sit idle most of the day. Resizing on a schedule requires building and maintaining Lambda functions and a schedule yourself, which violates the constraint of not creating new manual work. Exporting results to CSV eliminates the dashboard's interactive queries and therefore does not match the requirement.

prompt: A data analytics company has several TB of Parquet objects (hundreds of MB per object) in its Amazon S3 data lake. Some partitions are not queried for weeks and are then suddenly queried heavily at quarter close. The access pattern is unpredictable, the company must avoid separate retrieval charges every time data is queried, and it does not want the operational burden of constantly adjusting lifecycle rules. Data must be readable immediately, with no restore wait time. Everything is currently in S3 Standard, and the data team has three people. During last year's quarter-close week, retrieval charges made the bill nearly double what was expected, and the finance team raised the issue. Which method meets these requirements and reduces storage cost MOST efficiently?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create a lifecycle rule that transitions objects to S3 Standard-IA, and have an owner manually tag the objects used at quarter close so that they are excluded from the rule.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Transition objects to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 30 days, and separately operate an AWS Lambda function that runs bulk restore requests before quarter close. Each restore request incurs a retrieval charge and takes several hours to complete.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Store objects in S3 One Zone-IA and review the S3 Storage Lens report every month to have a person change the storage class of objects manually.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Store objects in the S3 Intelligent-Tiering storage class so that objects automatically move between tiers based on access frequency and no retrieval charges apply when they are queried.

explanation: The correct answer is to store the objects in S3 Intelligent-Tiering. When the access pattern changes, objects move between tiers automatically, this class has no retrieval charges, and an object in a lower tier that is read again returns to the Frequent Access tier. This satisfies all three constraints: unpredictable patterns, avoiding retrieval charges, and low operational burden. The Standard-IA and manual tagging approach incurs retrieval charges based on query volume and requires an owner to keep intervening. Glacier Flexible Retrieval requires restoring objects before reading them, which does not fit sudden bursts of queries and also requires operating restore automation. One Zone-IA requires people to make changes based on access patterns, so it does not meet the automatic optimization requirement.

prompt: A startup wants to create dozens of new analytics tables in Amazon Redshift. The tables currently have tens of thousands of rows but could grow to hundreds of millions of rows in a few months, and the query patterns are not yet known because the product has not launched. There is only one data engineer, who wants to minimize the operational burden of continually reviewing and changing distribution keys and sort keys. The table DDL must be written now, and even if the query patterns become clear later, the company wants to avoid recreating tables manually as much as possible. The BI tool uses only standard SQL and does not depend on the query plans that Amazon Redshift generates. How should the tables be created?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create all tables with DISTSTYLE ALL so that no join requires data movement, and keep the same style even after the tables grow.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Set the distribution style and sort keys to AUTO so that Amazon Redshift observes table size and query patterns and automatically adjusts the distribution style and keys.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create all tables with DISTSTYLE KEY from the start with the first column fixed as the distribution key, and have a person change it when a problem appears.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Specify an INTERLEAVED sort key for each table, schedule VACUUM REINDEX weekly, and have a person periodically reevaluate the effect of the sort keys.

explanation: The correct answer is to set the distribution style and sort keys to AUTO. AUTO distribution starts with ALL for small tables and changes to KEY or EVEN in the background as they grow, and automatic table optimization observes query interactions and applies keys, so no manual tuning is needed. Keeping all tables as ALL means that when a table reaches hundreds of millions of rows, every node holds a full copy, greatly increasing storage space and load time. Fixing the first column as the distribution key means a person must detect and fix any data skew. Interleaved sort keys and periodic REINDEX actually increase the manual review work.

prompt: An ad tech company runs a daily batch Spark pipeline on an Amazon EMR cluster. The load varies greatly during the day, so a fixed-size cluster is under-provisioned during the day and idle at night. The cluster must automatically scale in and out between a minimum of 2 and a maximum of 100 instances. To protect core data and keep the primary node stable, On-Demand Instances are limited to a maximum of 10, and the company wants to cover the remaining growth with Spot Instances to reduce cost. The job runs on EMR 7.x, and the team does not want to maintain scaling scripts on its own. The cluster starts at night and ends in the morning, and the owning team does not want to decide cluster size directly in the console. Which configuration is MOST suitable?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Turn on EMR managed scaling, specify a minimum of 2, a maximum of 100, and an On-Demand limit of 10, and leave Spark dynamic resource allocation at its default (enabled).

choices.label: B
choices.text: Turn off Spark dynamic resource allocation to fix the number of executors, and raise only the managed scaling maximum to 100 so that the cluster grows as much as needed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group yourself and attach it to the EMR core nodes, and use a scale-in policy to terminate nodes when CPU utilization is low.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Schedule a script with Amazon EventBridge that terminates the cluster twice a day and recreates it at the new size, running 100 instances during the day and 2 at night.

explanation: EMR managed scaling is the correct answer. This feature watches cluster metrics and automatically adjusts the number of core and task nodes within the minimum and maximum range, and when an On-Demand limit is specified, it uses On-Demand Instances up to that limit and fills the rest with Spot Instances (with a minimum of 2, a maximum of 100, and a limit of 10, On-Demand is used up to 10 instances). Turning off Spark dynamic resource allocation can cause the cluster to grow to maximum capacity more than needed, so it is recommended to keep it enabled. EMR core nodes are not attached directly to EC2 Auto Scaling groups. Terminating and recreating the cluster is risky for running jobs and HDFS data and imposes a heavy operational burden.

prompt: A data analytics company's data lake bucket (hundreds of millions of objects) is encrypted with SSE-KMS using a customer managed AWS KMS key. Amazon Athena and AWS Glue read objects in bulk, and AWS KMS request costs have risen significantly this quarter. The security team requires that key policy-based access control and AWS CloudTrail auditing of key usage be maintained, and it has not approved moving the data to another bucket. The company also wants to reduce AWS KMS call costs for existing objects, and the query and ETL code cannot be modified. Versioning is turned off for the objects, and rewrite operations can be run overnight. The audit report must prove which principal read which object. Per-object evidence is already obtained from the S3 data event CloudTrail logs that are enabled, and only key usage principal and key-level auditing are required from KMS events (the security team has accepted that using a Bucket Key causes the bucket ARN rather than the object ARN to be recorded in KMS events). What is the MOST appropriate method?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enable an S3 Bucket Key on the bucket, and rewrite existing objects with CopyObject or similar so that they are re-encrypted with the Bucket Key.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An S3 Bucket Key applies to all existing objects as soon as it is enabled, so turn on only the bucket setting and take no additional action.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Change the default encryption from SSE-KMS to SSE-S3 so that Amazon S3 does not call AWS KMS, and keep encryption in place with S3 managed keys.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Turn on Athena query result reuse so that the same objects are not read repeatedly, in the hope that the number of AWS KMS calls decreases.

explanation: The correct answer is to enable an S3 Bucket Key and re-encrypt existing objects. A bucket-level key reduces the requests that Amazon S3 sends to AWS KMS and lowers cost, while key policy-based control and the AWS KMS CloudTrail key usage records are maintained. However, according to the official documentation, enabling a Bucket Key causes the bucket ARN, rather than the object ARN, to be recorded in AWS KMS CloudTrail events, and the number of events also decreases. For that reason, this question assumes that per-object read evidence is obtained from S3 data events. The setting applies only to objects written after it is enabled, so existing objects must be rewritten with CopyObject. Switching to SSE-S3 would lose key policy control and key usage auditing. The assumption that simply turning on the setting applies to existing objects is wrong. Query result reuse applies only to Athena results and does not reduce AWS KMS calls from other reads such as AWS Glue.

prompt: An e-commerce company has an AWS Glue ETL job that moves customer data from a raw zone to a curated zone. The curated zone must not contain email addresses and mobile phone numbers in plain text, but analysts must be able to join events of the same customer by email value. The job runs on AWS Glue 4.0 Spark, the data is tens of millions of rows, restoring the original values is not required, and only the security team can access the raw zone. The development team has two people, so it wants to write as little code as possible and configure this in AWS Glue Studio, which it already uses. Analysts join by comparing hashed email values for equality and do not need to recover the original email. Which method meets these requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Change the settings so that when an Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery job finds an email address, it automatically converts that value to an encrypted form.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In the Detect PII transform, replace the detected email values with the same fixed string by using partial redaction or bulk masking, and store the result in the curated zone.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Drop the email and phone number columns from the curated table, and use AWS Lake Formation to block analysts from accessing the raw zone table.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In the Detect PII transform, select the email and phone number entities and replace the values with the SHA-256 hash action, and store the result.

explanation: The correct answer is the SHA-256 hash action of the Detect PII transform. Detected PII values are replaced with SHA-256 hash results, so the original text disappears, and the same email always yields the same hash, so it can be used as a join key. Masking that replaces values with a fixed string makes all values the same, so the join produces incorrect results. Dropping the columns leaves no key to join on, and blocking the raw zone with Lake Formation does not solve the join problem. Macie is a service that discovers and reports sensitive data and does not transform the values of objects.

prompt: The marketing analytics team at a B2B software company wants to import only the records newly created or changed each hour from the Salesforce Opportunity object into Amazon S3 and analyze them with Amazon Athena. Because of limited development staff, it does not want to maintain source API call code, authentication renewal, or pagination by itself, and the first run should import everything, after which only changes should be transferred. Currently, S3 contains only monthly manual export files of the same object, and the analytics team says it is fine if data is up to one hour late. The current analytics dashboard refreshes monthly, and the sales team complains that it cannot see the latest opportunity status. Which method has the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Have a Spark job on an Amazon EMR cluster connect to Salesforce over JDBC every hour, read the whole object, and overwrite the S3 path.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Register Salesforce as an AWS DMS source endpoint and create a CDC task to continuously replicate changes to an S3 target.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Call an AWS Lambda function on an Amazon EventBridge schedule to poll the Salesforce REST API, and store the last query time in Amazon DynamoDB.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Create a flow in Amazon AppFlow with Salesforce as the source and Amazon S3 as the destination, and choose incremental transfer for the scheduled trigger.

explanation: The correct answer is incremental transfer in an Amazon AppFlow scheduled-trigger flow. AppFlow connects to SaaS sources such as Salesforce without code, and when incremental transfer is chosen, it transfers only the records added or changed since the last successful run. Lambda polling requires you to maintain code for API calls, pagination, and state storage. AWS DMS targets database engines and does not support Salesforce as a source. A full read on EMR rereads the entire object every hour, which violates both the requirement to transfer only changes and the requirement for minimal operational overhead.

prompt: A retail company's data pipeline uses an AWS Step Functions Standard workflow to run AWS Glue jobs for 12 regions and then run an aggregation job. The regional jobs are independent of one another, aggregation must start only after all of them finish, and a delay in one region must not block the execution of other regions. If a regional job fails transiently, the company wants to retry up to 3 times with exponential backoff. The company does not want to create a separate polling AWS Lambda function to check status because of the maintenance burden, and the workflow definition is written directly in Amazon States Language. The aggregation job produces meaningful results only when the outputs of all 12 regions exist, and it runs once a day in the early morning. Which TWO configurations meet the requirements? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chain the regional Task states in series, and if any one fails, have a Catch restart the workflow from the beginning.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Use a Map state (or Parallel state) to run the regional AWS Glue jobs concurrently, and configure it to move to the aggregation state after all of them complete.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Make the workflow an Express type and run the regional jobs by using the .sync integration pattern that waits for the AWS Glue job to complete.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Call the AWS Glue StartJobRun state with the .sync pattern and define a Retry with MaxAttempts of 3 and a BackoffRate.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Call StartJobRun asynchronously, and repeatedly check for completion with a Wait state and a polling Lambda function that calls GetJobRun.

explanation: The correct answers are a configuration that runs the regional jobs concurrently with a Map (or Parallel) state, and a configuration that calls the AWS Glue job with the .sync pattern while defining a Retry. A Map state moves to the next state only after all branches finish, which guarantees the aggregation order, and the .sync integration waits until the job finishes, so no polling code is needed, and exponential backoff can be declared with Retry. Express workflows do not support the .sync and callback integration patterns. Serial chaining cannot run independent jobs in parallel, and restarting everything on failure wastes all 12 regions. A Wait state and a polling Lambda function conflict with the requirement not to use them.

prompt: A logistics company has an Amazon DynamoDB orders table with a partition key of CustomerId and a sort key of OrderId, holding hundreds of millions of items, and only about 1% of them are in the 'not shipped' state. The operations team queries the list of not-shipped orders per customer thousands of times a day, and it currently uses Scan with a filter, which makes read costs high. When an order is shipped, it must disappear from the not-shipped list. The table is already in production and cannot be recreated, the order recording code can be modified, and a small amount of eventual consistency delay is acceptable. Another team has reports that read the same table, so the existing key structure and attribute names cannot be changed. Which method reduces read cost the MOST while minimizing changes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add an isOpen attribute only to not-shipped orders, and create a GSI with CustomerId and isOpen as its keys and query it. When an order is shipped, delete that attribute so that the item drops out of the index.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Add a local secondary index (LSI) to the table with the status attribute as the sort key, and have per-customer Query operations apply a status filter expression to return only not-shipped items.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Add a status attribute to every order, create a GSI with status as the partition key, read all items with the value 'not shipped' at once, and split them by customer in the application.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Place a DAX cluster in front of the table and change Scan requests to go to the DAX endpoint so that on cache hits no table read capacity is consumed and frequently read lists are reused from the cache.

explanation: The correct answer is to use a sparse GSI. DynamoDB writes only items that have the index key attributes to the index, so if only not-shipped orders have isOpen, the index contains only about 1% of the items, making Query fast and cheap. Deleting the attribute at shipment removes the item from the index, which matches the requirement. An LSI can be defined only when the table is created, and a filter expression filters after reading, so it does not reduce read cost. A GSI with status as the partition key places every order in the index and concentrates requests on a key with few values, which also does not fit per-customer lookups. DAX still reads the table on a cache miss and adds a cluster to operate.

prompt: A retail company has a SPICE dataset in Amazon QuickSight Enterprise with Athena as the source (about 180 million rows, the last 2 years of sales history). It currently does a full refresh every morning, which takes a long time and incurs high Athena scan costs. The only rows that are actually modified or added are transactions within the last 7 days, and rows older than that do not change. The executive dashboard must keep SPICE's fast response, and the analyses and dashboard settings that reference the dataset must remain as they are. There are three analysts, SPICE capacity is sufficient, and only Athena query cost is a problem. Which method reduces refresh time and cost the MOST?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Switch from SPICE to direct query to eliminate the refresh job entirely and have the dashboard read from Athena every time it is opened.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increase the full refresh schedule from once a day to twice a day to reduce the amount of change handled per run and shorten each run.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Configure an incremental refresh with a 7-day look-back window based on the date column, so that only the last 7 days are queried again and the corresponding window in SPICE is replaced.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Delete and recreate the dataset so that no old rows remain in SPICE, and load the entire new dataset from scratch every day.

explanation: The correct answer is an incremental refresh with a 7-day look-back window. An incremental refresh queries the source only for inserts, deletes, and updates within the specified period, deletes the SPICE data for that window, and replaces it with the new results, so it queries only the last 7 days instead of 180 million rows. It is supported in Enterprise edition for SQL sources such as Athena. Direct query scans Athena on every dashboard view, which can actually increase cost and latency. Two full refreshes a day double the total cost. Deleting and recreating the dataset loses the settings and dashboard connections and continues to incur the full load cost.

prompt: A manufacturing group's data platform team uses AWS Lake Formation to manage more than 400 tables across 3 business units. Dozens of new tables are added every week, and the groups with access differ by business unit and by sensitivity. Currently, an owner grants individual permissions each time a table is created, and omissions and delays are frequent. The team wants to manage this at scale so that permissions are applied automatically once a classification is assigned, and access control must remain centralized in Lake Formation. Business unit reorganizations happen every quarter, and there are two permissions administrators. The audit team requires being able to explain with consistent rules who can read tables of which sensitivity. Which method is MOST suitable?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add business unit prefix access rules to the S3 bucket policy, and operate with Lake Formation permissions left open to all principals.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create an IAM user group for each business unit, attach AWS Glue and Amazon S3 permissions directly as inline policies, and modify the policies when tables are added.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Automate a script that grants SELECT permission to each table by using the named resource method, and run it every time a new table is created.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Define LF-Tags (business unit, sensitivity), attach them to databases, tables, and columns, and grant permissions to principals based on tag expressions.

explanation: The correct answer is LF-Tag-based access control (LF-TBAC). If attributes such as business unit and sensitivity are defined as tags and permissions are granted to principals that match tag expressions, existing permissions apply automatically just by tagging a new table, which scales well to hundreds of tables. Named resource permissions require individual grants per table, so an automation script must be maintained continuously. Putting rules in a bucket policy and leaving Lake Formation open defeats centralized governance. IAM inline policies must be edited each time tables are added, and column-level control is also difficult.

prompt: A claims table managed by AWS Lake Formation at an insurance company contains claims data for all regions and a resident registration number column. A group of regional analysts must be able to see only the rows for their own region (region = KR) and must not be able to see the resident registration number column. They query with Amazon Athena, and the company does not want to create copies of the data or per-region tables because of cost and synchronization burden. More regions may be added in the future, and the audit team required that access control must not depend on the goodwill of the query author. The security team said that several other analyst groups already read the same table, so existing permissions must be maintained. Which method has the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Allow the analyst role to read the claims prefix through an Amazon S3 bucket policy, and create an Athena view that masks the resident registration number column.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create copies of the S3 prefix and tables for each region, and use IAM policies to restrict each analyst group to reading only its own region prefix.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create a data filter that specifies both a row filter expression and exclusion of the resident registration number column, and use that filter to grant SELECT permission to the analyst group.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Exclude only the resident registration number with a column-level filter, and instruct analysts through internal guidelines to write their own region in the WHERE clause of every query to restrict rows.

explanation: The correct answer is to attach a data filter that specifies both a row filter and column exclusion to a SELECT permission. A filter with both column and row conditions creates cell-level security, and Lake Formation-integrated engines such as Athena apply it at query time, so no copies are needed. Per-region copies create data duplication and pipeline management burden. Combining S3 bucket policies and views allows direct object reads that bypass Lake Formation permissions, and control becomes fragmented. Leaving the row restriction to a user convention is not enforced and does not meet compliance requirements.

prompt: A global e-commerce company must verify that postal_code is not empty only for rows in its order data where the country column is 'KR'. Postal codes for rows from other countries may be empty. Millions of order records per day are loaded by an AWS Glue ETL job, and the company wants to see the validation results as AWS Glue Data Quality evaluation results. It wants to handle this with a single AWS Glue Data Quality rule in AWS Glue 4.0, without adding a separate transform step that filters the data first. Rule evaluation must run inside the AWS Glue ETL job, because if one batch arrives late, the pipeline is delayed. Which DQDL rule MOST appropriately meets the requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Use (ColumnValues "country" != "KR") or (IsComplete "postal_code") as a composite rule and use the default evaluation method.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Use IsComplete "postal_code" and IsComplete "country" as a composite rule to check that both columns are populated.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Use the rule IsComplete "postal_code" where "country = 'KR'" to check postal code completeness only for KR rows.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Add the rule ColumnValues "country" = "KR" with threshold > 0.99 to check the ratio of rows subject to the postal code check.

explanation: The IsComplete rule with a where clause is the correct answer. In AWS Glue 4.0, DQDL lets you append a where clause with a SparkSQL condition enclosed in quotation marks after a rule so that only rows matching the condition are validated, and rows excluded by the filter are marked as passing. The composite rule that combines conditions with OR is evaluated by default on each rule across the whole column and then combined, so it cannot express a row-level condition and might fail unexpectedly. Requiring completeness of both columns would also treat empty postal codes of other countries as failures. A rule that checks the ratio of country values does not check postal codes at all.

prompt: An Amazon S3 bucket in account A of a healthcare company is encrypted with SSE-KMS using a customer managed AWS KMS key. A bucket policy allows s3:GetObject for an analytics role in partner account B, but when the account B role reads objects, a KMS-related AccessDenied error occurs. The partner role must use the key only to read objects in this bucket, and the security team's policy is that account A cannot hand the key to another account or replace the key itself. The two accounts belong to different AWS Organizations organizations. The analytics role in account B is read-only and does not write objects or perform key management operations. Which method resolves the problem while maintaining least privilege?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add kms:Decrypt for the account A key ARN only to the IAM policy of the account B role, and leave the key policy at its default.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Change the encryption key to an AWS managed key (aws/s3) so that account B can decrypt objects with the same AWS managed key.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Allow kms:Decrypt for the key in both the account A key policy and the IAM policy of the account B role.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Add a statement that allows kms:Decrypt for the account B role to the bucket policy so that object and key permissions are granted at once.

explanation: The correct answer is to allow kms:Decrypt in both the key policy and the IAM policy in account B. For cross-account AWS KMS use, the key policy must grant permission to the external account (or its role), and the external account's IAM policy must delegate it to users and roles, and either one alone is not enough. A bucket policy covers only Amazon S3 permissions and cannot grant AWS KMS key permissions. An AWS managed key's key policy cannot be changed, so it cannot grant permissions to another account. Adding only an IAM policy still results in denial because the key policy does not allow the external account.

prompt: A marketing data company has an AWS Glue Spark ETL job (AWS Glue 4.0, 20 G.2X workers) that runs every night. The result is needed only by the afternoon of the next day, so it is acceptable if the start is delayed by several hours or the number of workers changes during the run. This job has no dependencies on other jobs in the pipeline and is idempotent, meaning rerunning it produces the same result. There is a cost reduction goal, but the team has no time to rewrite the script. Job logging and notification settings are already configured and will not be changed, and the cost report is reviewed monthly. Which is the MOST appropriate way to reduce job cost without changing the script?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Change the job settings to extend the job timeout to 7 days so that no additional charges are incurred even if the job takes a long time.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Change the execution class of the job to FLEX so that it runs on spare capacity and is billed only for the time workers actually run.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Upgrade the worker type from G.2X to G.12X to try to reduce overall job cost in proportion to the shorter run time.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Change the job type to Python shell and write a new script that does not use a Spark cluster, eliminating the cost.

explanation: The correct answer is the FLEX execution class. It is an option for jobs that are not time-sensitive, available with AWS Glue 3.0 and later on G.1X and G.2X workers, and in exchange for start times and worker counts that can vary, it is billed by per-worker run time, lowering cost without script changes. G.12X does not support FLEX, and using larger workers raises the hourly cost. A Python shell job requires rewriting the script and is hard to substitute for large-scale Spark processing. Extending the timeout does not reduce cost and may actually increase charges if the job runs longer.

prompt: An online gaming company receives about 30,000 payment events per second through Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. For fraud detection, it must perform per-user sliding-window aggregation over the most recent 1 minute and stateful pattern detection across multiple events within a few seconds. Events arrive as JSON, and the processing results are delivered to an alerting system. The number of events can increase several times during event seasons. The company does not want to manage server clusters, and the development team is familiar with Java and SQL. Currently, payment events are analyzed only once a day in a batch, so fraudulent transactions are not discovered until the next day. Which configuration is MOST suitable?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Load data into Amazon S3 with Amazon Data Firehose, then run scheduled Amazon Athena queries every minute to calculate each user's payment totals for the most recent 1 minute.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink application reads the stream and performs window aggregation and stateful processing.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An AWS Lambda function is invoked for every record and stores each event in Amazon DynamoDB, and the 1-minute totals and patterns are calculated by queries at read time.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Run an Amazon EMR cluster continuously, and have a batch Spark job at 5-minute intervals read the stream data and perform per-user aggregation and pattern checks.

explanation: The correct answer is Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink. Flink is a stream processing engine that supports event-time windows and stateful operations, and as a managed service it requires no cluster operations and reads from Kinesis Data Streams directly. A combination of Firehose and Athena makes it hard to guarantee detection within a few seconds because of buffering and the query interval. A per-event Lambda function requires you to implement windows and state yourself, and calculating at read time causes large delays. A 5-minute batch on EMR does not meet the latency requirement and imposes a heavy burden of operating an always-on cluster.

prompt: The payments table in a fintech company's Amazon Redshift provisioned cluster has a card number column. The payment support team role (support_role) should see only the last 4 digits when assisting customers, and the audit team role must be able to see the full number. The payment app writes to this table directly, so the company cannot change the table data or create per-team copies or views. It wants only the value that is visible at query time to differ by role, the column must continue to exist, and the existing SELECT query statements of the support team must not change. The security team also wants to manage the history of configuration changes. The payment system already uses a role-based permission model in Amazon Redshift, and the audit team requires the change history of masking policies. Which method is MOST suitable?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create a separate table containing only the last 4 digits by using UNLOAD and COPY, and expose it by granting query permission on that table only to support_role.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Encrypt the card number column on the client side with AWS KMS before loading, and hide it by not giving support_role the decryption permission.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create a dynamic data masking policy that keeps only the last 4 digits of the card number column and attach it only to support_role.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Apply a column-level GRANT that revokes SELECT permission on the column from support_role so that the support team cannot query the card number column.

explanation: The correct answer is a dynamic data masking (DDM) policy. DDM masks or partially shows values per role at query time without changing the stored data, and a policy can be attached only to specific roles, so the support team sees the last 4 digits and the audit team sees the full number. A column-level GRANT either shows or hides the entire column and cannot do partial exposure. A separate table is the copy that the requirements ruled out and creates a data synchronization burden. Client-side encryption does not satisfy the requirement to expose only the last 4 digits and requires changing both the load and query code.

prompt: A game company wants to export data from an Amazon DynamoDB provisioned table (about 4 TB, with read capacity set for normal service traffic) to Amazon S3 every early morning and analyze it with Amazon Athena. It currently uses a script that reads the table with Scan, and service read requests have been throttled while it runs. The analytics queries are needed only between 2 AM and 4 AM, and a daily snapshot of the data is sufficient. There is no budget to permanently raise read capacity, and the service code cannot be modified. The data team received budget approval on the condition that read capacity cost does not increase this quarter. Which method does not affect the service's read performance and has low operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increase the number of parallel segments in the Scan script and raise the table read capacity to twice the normal level only during the early morning hours to absorb throttling.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Turn on DynamoDB Streams, write all changes to S3 files with AWS Lambda, load the initial 4 TB once with Scan, and continuously merge the changes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Attach a DAX cluster to the table and change the Scan script to read from the DAX endpoint so that the table is not read on cache hits.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Turn on point-in-time recovery for the table and use the DynamoDB export to Amazon S3 feature. This export does not consume the table's read capacity.

explanation: The correct answer is to turn on PITR and use export to Amazon S3. Export requires PITR to be enabled, runs asynchronously, and does not consume read capacity (RCUs), so it has no effect on table performance. The results are stored in S3 in DynamoDB JSON or Ion format and can be read with Athena. Raising capacity for a parallel Scan uses more read capacity, so it keeps competing with service requests and also increases cost. A Streams and Lambda merge requires a lot of code to build and operate. DAX reads the table on cache misses, offers little benefit for a job that reads the entire 4 TB every day, and adds a cluster to operate.

prompt: A logistics company's data team operates 80 DAGs on an on-premises Apache Airflow 2.x server, using custom Python operators and third-party provider packages. The operations staff currently consists of only two people. Server patching and scheduler failure response take a lot of time, so they want to move to AWS, the migration must be finished within two months before the year-end settlement season, and DAG code should be modified as little as possible. The data that the DAGs read is already in Amazon S3 and Amazon Redshift. The current server is patched monthly, which repeatedly halts DAG runs and causes strong complaints from the team. Which method has the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create an Amazon MWAA environment and upload the DAG files, requirements.txt, and plugins to an S3 bucket to run the existing code almost as is.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Rewrite the 80 DAGs in the Amazon States Language of AWS Step Functions state machine definitions and newly implement the custom operators as AWS Lambda functions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Install Airflow yourself on two Amazon EC2 instances, wrap it with an Auto Scaling group and a load balancer, and operate it the same way as before while preparing for scheduler failures.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Move the DAG dependencies to AWS Glue workflows and triggers, and reimplement everything the custom operators did as AWS Glue jobs.

explanation: The correct answer is Amazon MWAA. MWAA is managed Apache Airflow, where AWS operates the scheduler and web server, and because DAGs, requirements.txt, and plugins are uploaded to S3, existing DAG code needs almost no modification. Rewriting in Step Functions would require redeveloping all 80 DAGs and the custom operators. Installing on EC2 yourself would carry over the current burdens of patching and failure response. AWS Glue workflows cannot replace the Airflow operator ecosystem, so all operator logic would have to be reimplemented.

prompt: A retail company's Amazon Redshift cluster holds the most recent 13 months of sales data. The preceding 5 years (about 400 TB, Parquet, partitioned by date) are in Amazon S3 and registered in the AWS Glue Data Catalog. Analysts need to join historical data with recent data a few times each quarter, but the company wants to avoid reloading historical data into the cluster because of storage cost and load jobs. It wants to keep using its existing Amazon Redshift SQL tools for writing queries and has no staff to adopt a new analytics service. Analysts mostly query only recent data and use historical data only for year-over-year trend analysis. Which method meets the requirements with minimal changes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Connect an Amazon Redshift Spectrum external schema to the AWS Glue Data Catalog to query the historical data in S3 directly as external tables and join them with local tables.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Load all 400 TB of historical data into Amazon Redshift with COPY, increase the number of nodes, and manage it combined with the recent data in a single table.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Have analysts query historical data with Amazon Athena, download the results as CSV, and upload them to an Amazon Redshift temporary table to join whenever needed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Copy the historical data in S3 to Amazon DynamoDB daily with AWS Glue ETL, and have Amazon Redshift read the DynamoDB table with a federated query to join with recent data.

explanation: The correct answer is to query S3 data directly as external tables with Amazon Redshift Spectrum. Spectrum can query S3 files and join them with local tables without loading the data into Amazon Redshift, and it uses the existing AWS Glue catalog and Parquet partitions as they are, so it requires the fewest changes. Loading 400 TB creates storage cost and load jobs, directly violating the constraints of the question. Having analysts manually upload Athena results involves a lot of repetitive work and data movement for every join, making it hard to operate. Copying to DynamoDB creates a pipeline that moves 400 TB again and adds the cost of a new data store.

prompt: A SaaS company loads order events (JSON, about 5,000 per second) into Amazon S3 with Amazon Data Firehose. Analysts mainly run Amazon Athena queries that filter by tenant_id and event date and want to reduce the amount of data scanned. Currently only a prefix based on arrival time is used, and there are hundreds of tenants and the number keeps growing. The company wants to split S3 prefixes by the tenant_id value in the record content while keeping separate compute code and after-the-fact reprocessing jobs to a minimum. The producer application is already deployed and will not be modified this quarter. Most Athena queries read the most recent month of data for a single tenant. Which method is MOST suitable?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Run an AWS Glue crawler every hour and configure it to relocate S3 objects to the appropriate prefixes based on the tenant_id column.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Turn on Firehose dynamic partitioning and use inline parsing to extract tenant_id from the record as a partition key and reflect it in the S3 prefix.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Invoke an AWS Lambda function on S3 object creation events to read the object, copy it again to a prefix per tenant_id, and delete the original.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Specify only year/month/day expressions based on arrival time in the prefix, and have the Athena query filter on tenant_id in the WHERE clause.

explanation: The correct answer is Firehose dynamic partitioning. It extracts a key such as tenant_id from the streaming data and delivers directly to an S3 prefix for that key, so Athena can reduce the scan volume, and inline parsing can be used without separate code. An arrival-time prefix alone cannot split by record content, so a tenant_id filter reads all objects for the dates. Copying again with Lambda after object creation creates compute code and copy and delete costs. A crawler only registers schemas and partitions in the catalog and does not move S3 objects.

prompt: Users in analytics accounts that belong to the same AWS Organizations organization as a large enterprise's central data account must query the AWS Glue Data Catalog and Amazon S3 data lake (managed by AWS Lake Formation) in the central account with Amazon Athena. Data will not be copied because of storage cost and duplicated governance, only specific databases should be accessible from the analytics accounts, and the company wants to centralize permission management in Lake Formation. More analytics accounts will be added in the future, and the security team prohibits sharing personal credentials. The central data team wants to retain catalog ownership and give users in the analytics accounts read-only permissions. What is the correct procedure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Copy the data to a bucket in the analytics account with an S3 replication rule, and then configure separate Lake Formation permissions from scratch within the analytics account.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Allow s3:GetObject for the entire analytics account through the S3 bucket policy in the central account, and define AWS Glue tables with the same schema directly in the analytics account.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The central account grants database permissions to the analytics account, and the analytics account administrator creates a resource link and grants permissions again to the analyst role.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Create an IAM user for analysts in the central account and share the credentials with users in the analytics accounts so that they use Athena in the central account.

explanation: The correct answer is Lake Formation cross-account grants and resource links. When permissions are granted to an external account, the resource is shared through AWS RAM, and within the same organization it can be used immediately. For integrated services such as Athena to include the shared resource in queries, a resource link is needed, and the administrator of the receiving account grants permissions again to users. Opening access only through a bucket policy skips Lake Formation permissions and catalog sharing, violating the centralization requirement and duplicating table definitions. Replicating data violates the condition of not copying. Sharing credentials conflicts with auditing and the principle of least privilege.

prompt: A mobile service company performs a full export of an Amazon DynamoDB table (PITR enabled, about 10 TB) to Amazon S3 every day to refresh its analytics data lake. Daily changes are less than 1% of the total, yet every time the company pays the charge for a full 10 TB export and the processing time. The analytics team is fine with freshness within a day, and the export job runs in the early morning. The service has tight read capacity, so the export must not affect the table's read capacity, and the company does not want to newly operate separate stream infrastructure to retain change history. The export results are queried with Amazon Athena and must keep the same schema, so format changes are not allowed. Which method reduces cost the MOST?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Run Scan in parallel, but create a script with a filter expression on a last-modified timestamp attribute so that only items changed since yesterday are read.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Switch the table to on-demand capacity mode to lower the full export charge, and reduce the export frequency to once a week.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Turn off PITR and query the daily backup files of AWS Backup directly with Athena to eliminate the export job itself.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Perform a full export once, and from then on run an incremental export every day that exports only the data changed in a specified time interval.

explanation: The correct answer is to use incremental exports after a full export. DynamoDB export supports both full and incremental exports, incremental exports are billed on the size of data processed from the continuous backup for the specified period, and they do not consume read capacity. A Scan with a filter expression reads the entire table regardless of the filter, consuming read capacity and costing a lot. Changing the capacity mode does not change the export charge basis, and reducing frequency only worsens the refresh cycle. Backup files cannot be queried directly with Athena, and export requires PITR to be enabled, so the option of turning PITR off does not work.

prompt: At an e-commerce company, a daily report in an Amazon Redshift cluster that joins a 2-billion-row orders table and a 50-million-row customers table on customer_id is getting slower. The execution plan shows a step (DS_DIST_BOTH) that heavily redistributes data from both tables between nodes on every join. Both tables are large tables whose order and customer information is frequently updated throughout the day, and the number of nodes will not be increased. The distribution style of both tables is currently EVEN. The report runs at 6 AM every day, and the same query is sometimes run manually several times a day. Which method MOST effectively reduces data redistribution during the join?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Change the customers table to DISTSTYLE ALL so that every node has a full copy, assuming that frequent updates do not affect load and update times. Accept that storage space grows because replicas increase with the number of nodes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Change both tables to DISTSTYLE KEY and specify customer_id as the distribution key so that rows with the same customer_id value are placed on the same slice.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Change both tables to DISTSTYLE EVEN so that rows are spread evenly across all slices in a round-robin fashion, independent of the join key.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Add customer_id only as a sort key on the orders table and leave the distribution style as is so that rows with the same value are read close together during the join.

explanation: The correct answer is to distribute both tables by KEY on customer_id. When two tables are distributed on the join key, rows with the same value are collocated on the same slice, so no redistribution is needed during the join. Replicating the 50-million-row customers table with ALL increases storage by the number of nodes, and according to the documentation, ALL is not suitable for frequently updated tables and makes loads and updates much slower. EVEN scatters rows regardless of the key, so redistribution remains during the join. A sort key only narrows the range of blocks to read and does not determine which node rows are placed on, so it cannot eliminate DS_DIST_BOTH.

prompt: A manufacturing company must continuously apply changes from an on-premises Oracle database (about 2 TB) to an Amazon S3 data lake. After a one-time full load, it must continue with the changes, and a downstream merge job must be able to tell whether each row was inserted, updated, or deleted. The source database has a high load during business hours, so the query load must be kept small, and the storage format must be favorable for analytics. On-premises and AWS are connected with AWS Direct Connect, and the DBA has already turned on archive log mode. Change history may be reflected up to one hour late, but deleted rows must not be missed. Which configuration is MOST suitable?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In an AWS DMS CDC task, set cdcInsertsOnly to true so that only insert records among the changes are written to S3 and the rest are ignored, on the assumption that this minimizes the source load.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Run an AWS Glue JDBC job every night to read and overwrite the entire table and infer deleted rows by comparing with the previous snapshot.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Move the initial 2 TB with AWS Snowball Edge, and afterward periodically create files of the changes in the same way, send them, and merge them.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Create an AWS DMS task of the full load and CDC type, set the S3 target to Parquet, and use the I/U/D indicator in the first field of the CDC records for merging.

explanation: The correct answer is an AWS DMS task that combines full load and CDC with a Parquet target. During CDC, AWS DMS by default writes I (insert), U (update), or D (delete) in the first field of the record so that the merge job can distinguish the operation type, and Parquet is favorable for analytics. A full JDBC read every night puts a large load on the source and cannot directly detect deletions. Snowball is only for the initial migration and has no means of ongoing change capture. cdcInsertsOnly writes only inserts, so updates and deletes are lost, which violates the requirements.

prompt: The Athena workgroup adhoc at a consulting company is used by 40 analysts, and queries that scan tens of TB without partition conditions occasionally run, causing monthly cost spikes. The company wants any query that scans more than 500 GB at a time to be stopped automatically, and does not want to build separate code or monitoring infrastructure. All analysts must keep using the same workgroup, and any change that alters the workgroup structure has not been approved. The administrator cannot respond in the early morning hours. The 500 GB limit was calculated by the finance team from the quarterly budget and will not be set differently per analyst. Which method has the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create a daily scan volume alarm at the workgroup level that notifies the administrator by using Amazon SNS, and have the administrator who receives the notification stop the query manually.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Receive AWS CloudTrail events through Amazon EventBridge, and when a query starts, have an AWS Lambda function calculate the expected scan volume and call StopQueryExecution if it exceeds the limit.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create 40 separate workgroups, one per analyst, and separate the query result location of each workgroup into a different S3 path.

choices.label: D
