choices.text: Set the per-query data usage control on the workgroup to 500 GB so that queries exceeding the limit are canceled automatically.

explanation: The per-query data usage control is the correct answer. This limit cancels any query in the workgroup whose scan volume exceeds the limit (minimum 10 MB), only one can be created per workgroup, and no additional configuration code is required. A workgroup-level alarm only sends an Amazon SNS notification when the total scan volume over a specified period exceeds a threshold and does not cancel queries automatically, so it does not meet the automatic stop requirement. Combining CloudTrail and Lambda requires building and operating code and infrastructure yourself. Splitting workgroups per person and separating result locations alone does not limit scan volume.

prompt: A data team creates a staging table (about 800 million rows) into which CSV files from Amazon S3 are first loaded with COPY in Amazon Redshift. The table is not joined with other tables; right after loading, the entire table is read once and inserted into a cleansed table with INSERT ... SELECT, and then it is emptied. There is no candidate key column with evenly spread values, and the load_date column has the same value in every row. The cluster consists of several RA3 nodes, and company standards require the distribution style to be specified explicitly. The goals are load speed and an even load across slices. The load job runs once overnight, and the staging table is emptied once cleansing is done. Which distribution style is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Specify DISTSTYLE EVEN so that rows are distributed evenly across all slices in round-robin fashion regardless of key.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Specify DISTSTYLE KEY with load_date as the distribution key so that rows with the same load date are collocated on the same slice.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Specify DISTSTYLE ALL so that every node has a full copy of all 800 million rows and the read in the cleansing step can occur on any node.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Specify DISTSTYLE KEY with the first column as the distribution key and configure it so that it is joined with the cleansed table on the same key after loading.

explanation: EVEN distribution is the correct answer. According to the documentation, with EVEN the leader node distributes rows across slices in round-robin fashion regardless of values, which is suitable when the table does not participate in joins or when there is no clear choice between KEY and ALL. KEY distribution on load_date would put all rows on a single slice, eliminating parallel processing and slowing loads. ALL replicates 800 million rows by the number of nodes, greatly increasing storage space and load time, and offers no benefit for a table that is not joined. KEY on the first column risks skew because there is no evenly distributed column, and since this table is not joined, there is no basis for it.

prompt: A financial company wants to use Amazon S3 lifecycle rules to move audit logs from Standard to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval 30 days after creation, and afterward to S3 Glacier Deep Archive as early as possible. The audit team says it occasionally needs immediate access for several months after the first 30 days, so the Instant Retrieval stage cannot be skipped. The rule applies to the whole bucket, and all object sizes are 128 KB or larger. The minimum storage duration for Glacier Instant Retrieval is 90 days, and moving objects to another tier before this period elapses incurs charges for the remaining period (according to the official documentation, a single rule cannot specify a transition before the minimum storage duration, and splitting it into two rules makes it possible but incurs the minimum duration charge). The finance team requires that no charges at all be incurred for not meeting the minimum storage duration. Which rule configuration meets this requirement with the earliest Deep Archive transition time?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Configure a rule that transitions to Glacier Instant Retrieval 30 days after creation and to Glacier Deep Archive 60 days after creation in a single rule.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Configure a rule that transitions to Glacier Instant Retrieval 30 days after creation and to Glacier Deep Archive 120 days after creation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Configure a rule that transitions to Glacier Instant Retrieval 30 days after creation and to Glacier Deep Archive 90 days after creation in a single rule.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Configure a rule that transitions to Glacier Instant Retrieval 30 days after creation and to Glacier Deep Archive 365 days after creation to satisfy the minimum storage duration.

explanation: The correct configuration transitions to Deep Archive on day 120, which is the 30-day Instant Retrieval transition plus the 90-day minimum storage duration. The official documentation (Constraints and considerations for transitions) explains that moving to another tier before the minimum storage duration incurs charges for the remaining period, that a single rule cannot specify a transition before the minimum duration (for example, if an object moves to Instant Retrieval on day 4, the Deep Archive transition must be at least 94 days later), and that splitting it into two rules makes it possible but incurs the minimum duration charge. The 60-day and 90-day transitions come before the 90 days in Instant Retrieval are complete, so they either cannot be created as rules or incur the minimum duration charge, which goes against the requirement. A 365-day transition has no charge but does not meet the requirement of as early as possible and keeps the objects in a more expensive tier for a long time.

prompt: A multi-tenant IoT platform sends sensor data to a provisioned-mode Amazon Kinesis stream (10 shards) and uses tenantId as the partition key. One large tenant accounts for 60% of all traffic, and WriteProvisionedThroughputExceeded errors repeatedly occur on a particular shard. The order of events for each sensor (deviceId) must be preserved because of the consumer's state calculation, and producer-side throttling must be resolved. Per-tenant lookups are handled on the consumer side by using the tenantId field in the event, so they are independent of shard placement. The producer specifies the partition key value directly in code, so the key generation method can be changed. What is the MOST appropriate solution?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Split only the hot shard that is being throttled, dividing its hash key range in half so that the load is shared by two shards.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create the partition key by appending a random suffix to tenantId on each record so that records of the same tenant are scattered across multiple shards, and minimally modify only the key generation part of the producer code.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Switch the stream to on-demand capacity mode so that shards increase automatically and can handle the traffic of a specific tenant.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Change the partition key to deviceId, which has high cardinality, so that records are distributed evenly across shards while the order for each device is also preserved.

explanation: The correct answer is to change the partition key to deviceId. The shard is determined by the hash of the partition key, so key cardinality must be high to spread the load, and records from the same device have the same key and therefore enter one shard in order. Switching to on-demand mode still sends the same tenantId key to a single shard, so the hot key problem remains. A random suffix distributes the load but scatters the records of the same device across multiple shards, breaking the order. Splitting the hot shard is not a fundamental fix either, because a single key hashes to one point and continues to be concentrated in one of the child shards.

prompt: A subscription service company has an AWS Glue ETL job that loads subscription events every day. Thanks to marketing campaigns, the number of events keeps growing, so the number loaded today should be greater than the average of the last 7 runs to be considered normal. The company currently uses a fixed threshold rule, but engineers must change the number each time the count grows, which is inconvenient, and missing an update hides anomalies. The job runs on AWS Glue 4.0, and validation results are checked as Data Quality evaluation results. The data team has already configured the pipeline that includes this validation to block downstream jobs when it fails. What is the MOST suitable way to implement this validation with AWS Glue Data Quality?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add a fixed threshold rule such as RowCount > 1000000, and have engineers manually raise the threshold number each time the count grows. If the threshold falls behind the trend, anomalies can be missed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Put RowCount in the Analyzers block and set a failure action option so that the job is stopped when the analyzer is lower than the average.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Attach with threshold > 0.9 to a ColumnValues rule to check whether at least 90% of the row values fall within the average range.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In the ruleset of the Evaluate Data Quality transform, add a dynamic rule such as RowCount > avg(last(7)) to compare with the average row count of the last 7 runs.

explanation: The RowCount dynamic rule is the correct answer. Dynamic rules reference metrics from previous runs by using the last() operator, and when several values are used, as in last(7), an aggregation function such as avg is needed, so RowCount > avg(last(7)) compares against the average of the last 7 runs. Dynamic rules are supported in AWS Glue ETL. A fixed threshold violates the constraint that people must keep changing it. Analyzers only generate statistics and cannot evaluate conditions or set an action that stops a job. The threshold of ColumnValues means the ratio of values that satisfy the condition, which is a different check from comparing row count trends.

prompt: An AWS Glue ETL job (using a JDBC connection inside a VPC) at a financial company must encrypt its Amazon S3 output, Amazon CloudWatch logs, and job bookmarks with a customer managed AWS KMS key. All three kinds of encryption are mandatory because of a compliance review. When a security configuration was attached to the job, it failed with a kms timeout error in a private subnet that has no internet route. Security policy does not allow a NAT gateway, and this subnet already has an S3 gateway endpoint. The network team approves adding endpoints. The job runs every day at 1 AM, and a security configuration is currently attached for log encryption and bookmark encryption. Which TWO actions allow the job to succeed while keeping the encryption requirements? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create an AWS KMS interface VPC endpoint and enable the private DNS name so that the job connects to AWS KMS from within the VPC.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Disable CloudWatch log encryption in the security configuration to reduce the AWS KMS call targets, leaving only S3 output encryption, and keep bookmark encryption as it is.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increase the job timeout and retry count to the maximum so that the job waits to the end even when AWS KMS responds slowly.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Add encrypt and decrypt permissions to the key policy so that the IAM role passed to the job and the CloudWatch Logs service can use the key.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Add the S3 gateway endpoint to the subnet route table so that AWS KMS requests are also forwarded to the same endpoint.

explanation: The correct answers are an AWS KMS interface VPC endpoint (with private DNS) and adding permissions to the key policy. When a security configuration is used with a JDBC job, AWS Glue needs a path to AWS KMS, and since a NAT cannot be used, a VPC endpoint is needed. In addition, the job role and the CloudWatch Logs service must be able to encrypt and decrypt with the key. Disabling log encryption violates the encryption requirement. An S3 gateway endpoint handles only S3 traffic and cannot serve as a path to AWS KMS. Increasing the timeout still results in timeout failures if there is no path.

prompt: A logistics company has an 8-shard Amazon Kinesis Data Streams stream that is read with the shared throughput method by four consumer applications (KCL 2.x): a real-time dashboard, anomaly detection, search indexing, and archiving. As consumers have been added, the delay from record arrival to processing has grown to nearly 1 second, and even if two or three more consumers are added within the quarter, the average latency must stay at tens of milliseconds. Producers cannot be changed, and consumer code changes must be kept to a minimum. The data retention period is currently 24 hours and will stay the same regardless of the latency problem. Of the four consumers, anomaly detection and the dashboard are latency-sensitive, and archiving is not. Which method meets the requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Extend the stream's data retention period to the maximum so that a slow consumer can catch up with every record later.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Merge the four consumers under the same KCL application name so that they share a single lease table and divide up the shards to read.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Register each consumer application as an enhanced fan-out consumer so that each uses dedicated read throughput per shard.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Split the stream's shards from 8 to 16 to double the total read throughput that the consumers can use together, and leave the consumer code as it is.

explanation: The correct answer is to register each consumer as an enhanced fan-out consumer. Enhanced fan-out provides each consumer with dedicated throughput of up to 2 MB/s per shard through HTTP/2 push, and the average propagation delay stays at about 70 ms whether there is 1 consumer or 5, and KCL 2.x can use it right away. Adding shards increases total capacity, but the shared method, in which several consumers split the 2 MB/s of a shard (about 1,000 ms with 5 consumers), stays the same, so it cannot guarantee the latency requirement. Extending retention only keeps data longer and does not reduce latency. Merging under the same application name makes the consumers split the shards, so each function would not receive every record.

prompt: A data team at an advertising company wants to validate and transform about 2 million CSV files under one prefix in Amazon S3, each with an AWS Lambda function. The job must finish within a few hours before month-end settlement, so it must be processed in parallel at large scale, and even if some files fail because of format errors, the overall job must continue as long as the failures stay within a tolerated failure percentage. Custom orchestration code must be minimal, and the processing results are kept in Amazon S3. The validation Lambda function has already been written and takes a few seconds per run. Each file is a few MB in size, and there is no order or dependency among files. What is the MOST appropriate method?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Have one Lambda function list the prefix and asynchronously invoke another Lambda function for each file, and write your own aggregation code to check the numbers of successes and failures.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A Distributed Map state in a Standard workflow reads the S3 object list directly, invokes Lambda in parallel, and sets a tolerated failure percentage.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pass the list of 2 million files at once as the input of an inline Map state in AWS Step Functions and have it iterate through all of them in parallel inside the state machine.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Use a Distributed Map state in an AWS Step Functions Express workflow to build the same configuration and set a tolerated failure percentage to process the files in parallel.

explanation: The correct answer is a Distributed Map in a Standard workflow. It reads the S3 object list directly as input, runs child workflows in parallel at large scale, and lets you set a tolerated failure percentage, so almost no orchestration code is needed. Distributed Map is not supported in Express workflows. A self-built Lambda fan-out requires you to implement listing, retries, and failure aggregation in code. An inline Map is not suited to handling a list of 2 million items because of limits on state input size and concurrency.

prompt: An IoT platform processes Amazon Kinesis Data Streams records with an AWS Lambda event source mapping (batch size 100). When a single record with a corrupted format arrives because of an equipment firmware bug, the function keeps raising errors, the same batch is retried repeatedly, and processing of the following records on that shard stalls. Normal records must keep being processed, while problem records must be kept so they can be analyzed later, and operational overhead must be minimal. The function code has no per-record error handling, and the development team cannot make major code changes this week. The incident responder says that if they know the location of the failed record (shard and sequence number), they can retrieve the original within the stream retention period, and manual reprocessing is acceptable. How should this be configured?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Catch all exceptions in the function code and return success to prevent retries, and move on, leaving the contents of records that caused errors only in the logs.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Turn on BisectBatchOnFunctionError, limit the maximum retry attempts and the maximum record age, and send failed record information to an Amazon SQS on-failure destination.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Extend the data retention period of the stream to the maximum, and have the development team manually fix problem records and resend them before they expire.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reduce the batch size to 1 and raise ParallelizationFactor to 10 so that an erroring record does not block other records on the same shard.

explanation: The correct answer is to set batch bisecting (BisectBatchOnFunctionError) together with limits on retry attempts and record age, and to specify Amazon SQS as the on-failure destination. Splitting the batch in half on each retry isolates the problem record, and a record that exceeds the limits is discarded while its information is delivered to the failure destination, so the shard flows again. With the defaults (unlimited retries and record age), the shard is blocked until the record expires, so reducing the batch size to 1 would still retry the same record forever and would not solve the problem. Extending retention only keeps the blocked state longer. Swallowing exceptions and reporting success means problem records are not kept anywhere except the logs, which violates the requirement to keep them in a form that can be analyzed later.

prompt: A fintech company's AWS account has 120 Amazon S3 buckets, and some of them may contain customer credit card numbers in plain-text files. Old log dumps and CSV exports are mixed together, and even the security team does not know exactly which buckets contain them. The security team wants to automatically scan all buckets every week and be notified immediately if sensitive information is found, and does not want to write its own code that reads file contents or move data elsewhere. There are two security staff members, and notifications are received through an existing Amazon SNS topic and email. The scan results are used as evidence by the compliance team every quarter, so the location showing which object the finding came from must be retained. Which method has the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Schedule a weekly Athena query that reads all objects and finds card numbers with a regular expression filter, and send a notification if the result count is not 0.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Schedule an Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery job weekly and forward finding events to Amazon SNS through an Amazon EventBridge rule.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create an AWS Glue job for each bucket that searches for the card number pattern with a regular expression, publish the number of matches as an Amazon CloudWatch custom metric, and set an alarm.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Enable the Amazon GuardDuty S3 protection feature and configure it so that a security finding notification arrives when objects in a bucket contain sensitive card numbers.

explanation: The correct answer is a recurring Amazon Macie discovery job with event notifications. A Macie job analyzes S3 objects for sensitive data by using managed data identifiers, can be run once or on a recurring schedule with a defined scope, and its findings can be received as events and connected to notifications. An AWS Glue regular-expression job requires creating and maintaining code for each bucket. GuardDuty S3 protection is intended to detect anomalous access behavior and does not classify sensitive information in object contents. A full Athena scan reads all objects every week, incurring large scan costs, and is not suited to unstructured files.

prompt: A data analytics company needs to read frequently, starting this quarter, about 200 objects that it moved to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval with a lifecycle rule 3 years ago. All objects are larger than 128 KB, versioning is turned off, and the key names are referenced by other systems and must not change. The company tried to move these objects back to Standard with a lifecycle rule, but such a transition was not allowed. Restoration taking several hours is acceptable, and because there are few objects, a script can handle it. The restored temporary copy needs to be readable only for as long as it is needed, and permanent storage must be in Standard. What is the correct procedure to put the objects back in the S3 Standard class?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add a transition from Glacier Flexible Retrieval to Standard to the lifecycle rule and set the start days to 0 so that it applies immediately.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Use copy-object to specify the Standard class and overwrite the same key directly without a restore request, and make restore requests later only for objects that failed during copying.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Retrieve the objects in Glacier Flexible Retrieval with a separate Glacier vault API and then upload them again as new objects to an S3 Standard bucket.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Issue a restore request for each object to create a temporary copy, and then use a copy operation to overwrite the same object while specifying S3 Standard as the storage class.

explanation: The correct procedure is to restore, then overwrite with a copy that specifies the class. According to the documentation, the only lifecycle transition target for Flexible Retrieval objects is Deep Archive, so to change to another class, you must first create a temporary copy by restoring and then specify the desired storage class in a copy operation that overwrites it. A 0-day transition rule is an unsupported transition and is rejected. Copying without restoring fails because archived objects cannot be read. These objects can be accessed only through the S3 API and not through a separate Glacier service API, so the vault API approach does not work.

prompt: At a platform company, several teams publish Avro events to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, and consumer teams deploy the new schema first and then read the past messages remaining in the stream. Recently, a publisher added one required field, and a new consumer raised an error while parsing past messages. Going forward, the company wants to allow at registration time only the changes that let consumers using the new schema also read data of the previous version. The team already uses AWS Glue, must avoid operating separate servers or its own schema service, and both publishers and consumers are written in Java. Schema changes usually happen about once a month, and consumer teams deploy the new schema before the change. What is the MOST appropriate method?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Use AWS Glue Schema Registry with the compatibility mode set to FORWARD so that only changes that let consumers of the previous version read data with the new schema are allowed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Register the schema in AWS Glue Schema Registry, set the compatibility mode to BACKWARD, and have publishers and consumers use the registry library.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Have an AWS Glue crawler infer the schema daily from sample records of the stream and update the Data Catalog table, and have consumers refer to that table.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Use AWS Glue Schema Registry with the compatibility mode set to NONE, and check the impact through announcements between teams and code reviews whenever the schema changes.

explanation: The correct answer is AWS Glue Schema Registry with the BACKWARD compatibility mode. BACKWARD is the rule that a consumer must be able to read data of both the current and the previous schema versions, so adding a required field is rejected at registration because past messages lack that field, while adding an optional field is allowed. The registry is serverless, so there are no servers to operate. FORWARD checks the direction in which consumers of the previous version read new data, so it does not block adding a required field. A crawler only infers after the fact and does not block changes. NONE performs no compatibility check, so the same error would recur.

prompt: A data team updates a 3 TB Amazon S3 table, to which a new date folder (dt=YYYY-MM-DD) is added every day, with an AWS Glue crawler. The crawler rescans the entire path each time, so run time and cost keep growing. The same Data Catalog table is read by Amazon Athena, AWS Glue jobs, and Amazon Redshift Spectrum, and the existing schema does not change; only new partitions need to be registered. The team has three members and cannot afford to maintain newly written code, and the table location and name are referenced by other systems and cannot be changed. The catalog table changes only during one hour in the early morning, and other teams' queries start right after. What is the improvement method with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Build a custom registrar in which an AWS Lambda function lists the entire bucket when a date folder is created and calls AWS Glue BatchCreatePartition.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Change the crawler's recrawl policy to incremental crawl (crawl new folders only) so that only newly added partitions are registered in the catalog.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Change the schedule so that the crawler runs several more times a day, reducing the amount of new data to be scanned at one time.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Configure Athena partition projection and delete the crawler so that Athena computes the paths without registering catalog partitions.

explanation: The correct answer is an incremental crawl, which crawls only newly added folders and adds new partitions to the table. Because the condition says the schema does not change, an incremental crawl is suitable and requires no separate code. Increasing the run frequency keeps the structure of scanning everything each time, so cost actually rises. Partition projection is an Athena-only feature, so AWS Glue jobs and Redshift Spectrum, which read catalog partitions, would not find the partitions. A Lambda registrar takes on listing the whole bucket and code maintenance, which is a heavier operational burden.

prompt: A streaming service company has a producer that writes to an Amazon Kinesis Data Streams stream with the KPL, and a consumer application. In the last outage, the company learned only much later, through customer inquiries, both that the producer failed to write records and that the consumer fell behind. The team wants to detect with Amazon CloudWatch alarms, first, the case where the producer fails to write records, and second, the case where the consumer falls behind the end of the stream. The stream is in provisioned mode, and traffic varies by time of day. Alarm notifications are sent to the on-call engineer's SNS topic, and alarm thresholds are set by looking at normal traffic levels. Which TWO alarms are appropriate? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Raise an alarm, treating it as a write failure, when the Minimum statistic of IncomingBytes is 0.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Raise an alarm, treating the consumer as lagging, when the Minimum statistic of GetRecords.Latency exceeds a threshold.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Raise an alarm when the Average statistic of PutRecords.Success falls below a threshold.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Raise an alarm when the Maximum statistic of GetRecords.IteratorAgeMilliseconds exceeds a threshold.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Raise an alarm, treating it as a write problem, when the Maximum statistic of WriteProvisionedThroughputExceeded is 0.

explanation: The correct answers are the Average of PutRecords.Success and the Maximum of GetRecords.IteratorAgeMilliseconds. The official documentation recommends using PutRecords.Success when using the KPL and setting an alarm on the Average statistic to learn about write failures, and monitoring consumer progress with the Maximum of IteratorAgeMilliseconds. A Minimum of 0 for IncomingBytes means there were no writes for a moment, not that they failed. The Minimum of read latency does not indicate consumer lag. For the write throttling metric, 0 is normal and values above 0 are the problem, so the condition is reversed.

prompt: In an e-commerce company's pipeline that processes an Amazon Kinesis Data Streams stream (6 shards) with AWS Lambda, IteratorAge keeps rising as traffic grows. There are no function errors, and the bottleneck is the structure in which only one batch is processed at a time per shard because the function runs for a long time. The order of records with the same partition key must be preserved, and the function code cannot be changed this quarter. The number of shards can be changed in the stream settings, and some cost increase is acceptable. The average record size is currently small, but a single function execution takes several seconds, and there is headroom in the invocation limits. Which TWO methods reduce the delay? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Raise the ParallelizationFactor of the event source mapping from 1 so that a single shard is processed with several concurrent batches.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increase MaximumBatchingWindowInSeconds to 300 seconds so that records are gathered longer and processed at once.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increase the number of shards in the stream to raise the read and processing parallelism so that more batches are processed concurrently.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Extend the data retention period of the stream so that records are read before they expire even if processing is late.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Turn on BisectBatchOnFunctionError to add the behavior of splitting a batch in half and retrying when one batch fails.

explanation: The correct answers are raising the ParallelizationFactor and increasing the number of shards. ParallelizationFactor (up to 10) processes a single shard with several concurrent batches while guaranteeing order per partition key, and adding shards increases the number of batches processed at the same time. Extending the batching window to 5 minutes increases the time spent waiting for invocation, which makes the delay larger. Extending retention only delays record expiration and does not raise processing speed. Batch bisecting works only when function errors occur, and this situation has no errors, so it has no effect.

prompt: A media company's web servers send one-line CSV logs to an Amazon Data Firehose delivery stream. Logs keep arriving at hundreds of GB per day and the schema is fixed. The team wants to store the logs in Amazon S3 in Parquet format in a serverless way and query them with Amazon Athena, and does not want to create hourly manual batch jobs. The log output format of the web servers cannot be changed, and the team already uses the AWS Glue Data Catalog. A single record is a few hundred bytes, and the peak traffic hours of the day are known. Which TWO configurations meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: In the compression format option of the S3 destination, select Parquet so that Firehose compresses files into Parquet on delivery.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Connect an AWS Glue crawler directly to the Firehose stream so that it automatically creates column definitions from records entering the stream.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Define column names and types in an AWS Glue catalog table, specify it as the schema for Firehose format conversion, and output Parquet.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Specify CSV as the input format of Firehose record format conversion so that Firehose reads CSV directly without a separate transform.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Configure the Firehose data transformation AWS Lambda function to convert each CSV line into a JSON record and return it.

explanation: The correct answers are converting CSV to JSON with a transformation Lambda function and converting to Parquet by specifying an AWS Glue catalog table schema. Firehose format conversion works only when the input is JSON, so CSV must first be converted to JSON with Lambda, and the conversion needs a schema from the AWS Glue Data Catalog. CSV cannot be chosen as an input format. A crawler does not directly read a Firehose stream as a source. The compression options are compression methods such as GZIP and Snappy, and Parquet is set not as compression but through the format conversion feature.

prompt: An AWS Glue Data Quality ruleset at a membership service has the composite rule (ColumnValues "age" >= 26) OR (ColumnLength "name" >= 4). By default, each rule is evaluated separately against the entire dataset and then the results are combined. The team wants SQL-like behavior in which a row passes if it satisfies either of the two conditions, as well as row-level results. The job runs in AWS Glue 4.0 with the Evaluate Data Quality transform, and the team wants to adjust only the evaluation method without changing the meaning of the rule statements. The team currently stores rule evaluation results in Amazon S3 and wants row-level results to be written to the same location. How should this be configured?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Instead of grouping the two rules into a composite rule, change them to independent rules that each have with threshold > 0.5, and treat a row as having passed with only one of them if each rule passes more than half of the rows, checking the pass ratio per rule.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Move the composite rule to the Analyzers block so that the analyzer calculates per-row statistics, and combine the columns of the result table with OR yourself.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In the additionalOptions of EvaluateDataQuality, specify compositeRuleEvaluation.method as ROW so that composite rules are evaluated at the row level.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Change the OR operator to AND so that only rows that satisfy both conditions pass, and use this result as a substitute for row-level evaluation.

explanation: The correct answer is to set compositeRuleEvaluation.method to ROW. By default, composite rules evaluate each rule against the whole data and then apply the operator, but setting this option to ROW makes the composite rule evaluate whole rows as a single rule and also yields row-level results. Attaching a threshold to independent rules only looks at the satisfaction ratio of each and cannot combine them with OR in a single row. Analyzers cannot evaluate conditions. Changing OR to AND changes the required meaning, so a row would have to satisfy both conditions to pass.

prompt: A telecom company loads one gzip-compressed CSV file (about 400 GB) created daily by an upstream system into an Amazon Redshift provisioned cluster with 32 slices by using COPY. The file format and compression method are fixed by the upstream system and cannot be changed, and loading has been slow, like a single stream, for several hours, which delays the morning report. The file is already uploaded under one S3 prefix, and a preprocessing step that splits the file before loading can be added. The cluster size must be kept because of cost. The cluster handles BI queries during the day, so the load must finish in the early morning hours, and splitting a compressed file does not change its content. What should the company do to reduce load time?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Instead of COPY, run INSERT INTO ... SELECT statements concurrently from multiple sessions to insert split rows, assuming each session uses a different slice so the whole cluster loads in parallel.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Add only the COMPUPDATE OFF option to COPY to skip the compression encoding analysis step and leave the other settings as they are.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Split the compressed file into multiple files of similar size between 1 MB and 1 GB after compression, match the number of files to a multiple of the number of slices, and COPY from the same prefix.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Change the node type to a larger type to increase the cores and memory that read the single gzip file and raise the load speed for a single file.

explanation: The correct answer is to split the file into similar sizes and match the number of files to a multiple of the number of slices. Compressed CSV files such as gzip are not split automatically, so a single file is loaded serially, and the data must be divided into multiple files of 1 MB to 1 GB after compression so that slices read in parallel in the MPP architecture. A single gzip file is not split even if nodes are enlarged, so read parallelism does not increase. INSERT ... SELECT is not a way of reading S3 files and is less efficient than COPY for bulk loading. COMPUPDATE OFF only reduces the analysis time and does not address the root cause, which is serial reading.

prompt: A group of data engineers at a company creates and runs AWS Glue jobs directly. The account also has an administrator role and a role for accessing the billing system, in addition to the service role glue-etl-role that AWS Glue assumes. The security team wants engineers to be able to pass only the service role glue-etl-role to AWS Glue, and to prevent privilege escalation by attaching other roles with stronger permissions to a job. Engineers frequently need to create new jobs, so they must be able to create jobs without security team approval. All jobs run in the same account, and engineers already have glue:CreateJob and glue:StartJobRun permissions. What is the MOST appropriate IAM policy design?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Allow engineers iam:CreateRole and iam:AttachRolePolicy so that they create and use a dedicated role themselves each time they create a job, and distinguish role names by a prefix convention.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Attach AdministratorAccess to glue-etl-role so that no data job fails because of insufficient permissions, and instruct engineers to use only this role.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Allow iam:PassRole only for the glue-etl-role ARN and restrict it with an iam:PassedToService condition of glue.amazonaws.com.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Allow iam:PassRole on all resources in the engineer policy and control access only by restricting the scope of glue:CreateJob to a job name pattern, leaving role selection to the engineers.

explanation: The correct answer is to restrict iam:PassRole to a specific role ARN and to use the iam:PassedToService condition so that it can be passed only to AWS Glue. For a user to pass a role to a service, PassRole permission is needed, and restricting the Resource element to the approved role prevents privilege escalation by attaching a role with stronger permissions. If PassRole is opened to all resources, a job name restriction cannot control which role gets attached. Giving the role AdministratorAccess violates the principle of least privilege. Giving permissions to create roles and attach policies lets engineers elevate their own permissions.

prompt: A fintech company stores transaction data in Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL, and the analytics team builds dashboards in Amazon Redshift. Currently, an AWS Glue job that runs every 5 minutes moves the data, but it fails often whenever the schema changes, and reflection delays are long. The company wants to reflect changes in the production database in Amazon Redshift in near real time without creating and operating new pipeline code. Both services are in the same Region in the same account, and the data team has three people and cannot manage replication infrastructure on its own. The analytics team can tolerate a delay of a few minutes but not a delay of a day, and source write performance must not be affected. Which method has the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create a zero-ETL integration with Aurora PostgreSQL as the source and Amazon Redshift as the target so that changes are replicated automatically after the initial load.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create an AWS DMS replication instance yourself, configure a full load and change data capture task, and continuously manage the size and status of the replication instance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create a schedule that exports an Aurora snapshot to Amazon S3 every hour, and have AWS Step Functions run COPY when the export finishes. Because the entire snapshot is converted, the delay grows as the data grows.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Modify the application to additionally write an event to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams for every transaction, and load it into Amazon Redshift with Amazon Data Firehose.

explanation: A zero-ETL integration is the correct answer. When you specify the source and Amazon Redshift, replication happens automatically after the initial load, the integration status is monitored as a managed service, and it recovers by itself where possible when problems occur, so no pipeline code or operations are needed. AWS DMS can also replicate change data, but you must operate the replication instance and tasks yourself, so it loses on the operational overhead constraint. The snapshot export and COPY approach increases the delay to hours and requires building orchestration. Modifying the application to write events twice requires both application changes and operating a new streaming pipeline.

prompt: At a data-selling company, partners upload CSV files averaging 150 MB to Amazon S3 irregularly throughout the day (about 300 times a day). Within 5 minutes of upload, each file must be converted to Parquet with cleaned-up column types and stored under a different prefix. A single file can be processed in the memory of a single node, and there are no joins or aggregations between files. The company wants to minimize cost with no always-on infrastructure and keep the code simple. The partners' upload method cannot be changed. The transformation rules consist only of specifying column types and converting the file format, and there are also long periods during the day with no uploads. Which method is MOST suitable?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Start a new AWS Glue Spark job on every S3 object creation event to read the file with distributed Spark, transform it, and save the result as Parquet.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Run an Amazon EMR cluster continuously, and have a Spark Streaming job that polls the input prefix find new files and convert them to Parquet.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Invoke an AWS Lambda function on S3 object creation events, read the CSV with a pandas-based layer, and save it as Parquet.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Send the file contents to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, and then have Amazon Data Firehose format conversion deliver Parquet files to Amazon S3.

explanation: The correct answer is an AWS Lambda function invoked by S3 events with a pandas-based library. It is event-driven, so there is no idle cost, a 150 MB file can be handled in the memory of a single function, and the 5-minute limit is sufficient. Starting an AWS Glue Spark job for every file means startup and DPU charges that are excessive for small files that do not need distributed processing. A continuously running EMR cluster violates the condition of having no always-on infrastructure. A configuration that goes through Kinesis requires splitting file contents into records, making the code complex, and does not match the requirement of file-level conversion.

prompt: The finance team at a manufacturing group wants the FinOps team to be notified by email when the total daily scan volume of the Athena workgroup finance-bi exceeds 2 TB. However, during month-end closing hours, queries must not be stopped even if the threshold is exceeded. The notification target is a single shared mailbox address of the FinOps team, and the company does not want to write separate code. The workgroup already has a query result location and Amazon CloudWatch metrics publishing turned on. The response after receiving a notification is decided by the FinOps team using human judgment. The alert threshold is about 1.5 times the usual daily scan average, and the finance team reviews the value every quarter. What is the simplest configuration that meets these requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Set the per-query data usage control of the workgroup to 2 TB so that queries that reach the limit are canceled and an alert email is also sent. Assume that the per-query limit also monitors the combined daily scan volume.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Subscribe an AWS Lambda function that disables the workgroup to the SNS notification so that scan volume stops growing, and also send an email.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Subscribe the FinOps team by email to the AWS Cost Explorer monthly report so that they review Athena cost on a monthly basis.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Set a workgroup-level data usage alert with a daily threshold of 2 TB and specify an SNS topic with an email subscription. Queries are not canceled automatically when the threshold is reached.

explanation: A workgroup-level data usage alert is the correct answer. This alert sets a threshold on the hourly or daily aggregate scan volume and notifies through a CloudWatch alarm and Amazon SNS, and queries are not canceled automatically when the threshold is reached. The per-query limit cancels a query when its scan volume exceeds the limit, so it would stop queries during closing hours and violate the requirement. An AWS Lambda function that disables the workgroup would also block all subsequent queries. The monthly cost report cannot notify of a daily threshold being exceeded.

prompt: An AWS Glue ETL job at a healthcare data company reads data from Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. Security policy requires the database password to be changed every 30 days, and the password must not remain in plain text in scripts or job parameters. The job runs once a day, and connection information is managed with an AWS Glue connection object. The company wants no job code changes when the password changes, and rotation must not cause job failures. The infrastructure team has no staff to write a new rotation script. The RDS instance is in a private subnet, and AWS Glue already accesses it through a connection in the same VPC. What is the MOST appropriate method?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Place the password in a plain string parameter in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store and manually update the job parameter each time it is rotated.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Store the credentials in an AWS Secrets Manager secret, set up automatic rotation every 30 days, and have the AWS Glue connection reference that secret.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Put a value encrypted with AWS KMS into the script as a constant, and redeploy the script with a new value every rotation cycle.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Create a read-only database user, set its password not to expire, and keep using the value set once in the job settings.

explanation: The correct answer is an AWS Secrets Manager secret with automatic rotation and an AWS Glue connection that references the secret. If credentials are kept in Secrets Manager, automatic rotation for RDS meets the 30-day cycle, and because the AWS Glue connection references the secret, the script does not need to be changed after rotation, and the password is not exposed in plain text. A plain string in Parameter Store is plain text and needs manual updates. Putting an encrypted constant in the script requires deploying code at every rotation. A password that never expires violates the 30-day rotation policy.

prompt: A data engineer specified the job-bookmark-enable option on an AWS Glue Spark ETL job that reads an Amazon S3 path where new JSON files accumulate daily. However, every run rereads files that were already processed, so the output is duplicated on a daily basis and downstream aggregate values are inflated. Looking at the script, the read step has no transformation_ctx argument, and there is no job.commit() call at the end. The input path and job structure must not change, but the script can be modified. The job runs once a day, and previous output accumulates in date partitions, so duplicates are conspicuous when they occur. What is the MOST appropriate action to resolve the problem?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Specify transformation_ctx on the step that reads the data source and call job.commit() at the end of the script so that the bookmark state is saved.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reset the bookmark with reset-job-bookmark before starting every run to keep it clean so that no previous state remains.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Change the bookmark option to pause so that each run reads only data after the last successful point (do not modify the job script).

choices.label: D
choices.text: Double the number of workers in the job so that processing finishes sooner, which makes bookmark updates happen on time and removes the duplicates.

explanation: The correct answer is to specify transformation_ctx and call job.commit(). Bookmark state consists of entries per source, transformation, and sink, identified by the transformation context, and is saved atomically when job.commit() is called, so if either one is missing, the next run does not know the previous state and rereads the files. The pause option reads data after the last successful point but does not update the bookmark state, so it does not fix the problem. A reset erases the state, so each run actually rereads everything. The number of workers affects only processing speed and is unrelated to whether state is saved.

prompt: An AWS Glue job at an advertising company reads 2 TB of JSON logs per day and writes the transformed results to Amazon S3. This data is used for BI dashboards and ad hoc analysis queries, and most queries cover short time ranges. Analysts query only 4 of the 80 columns with Athena and mostly filter on the most recent 7 days. The data is currently stored as JSON, and query cost, which is proportional to scan volume, is exceeding the monthly budget. The storage format can be changed in the AWS Glue job, and the company does not want to change the analysts' query statements. The data retention period is 13 months, and even after switching to a new format, historical data does not need to be converted again. How should the output be stored to reduce scan volume and query cost the MOST?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Store it in Parquet format with Snappy compression and partition by event date so that date range queries read only the necessary partitions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Store it in Parquet format but without partitions, piling all dates under a single prefix, and let Athena select and read only the columns.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Store it as gzip-compressed JSON Lines files split by date prefix to reduce storage space so that date filters apply.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Store it in ORC format and partition by user ID, creating millions of partitions to favor per-user lookups.

explanation: The correct answer is Snappy Parquet partitioned by date. A columnar format reads only the 4 columns being queried and skips unnecessary blocks using block statistics, and date partitions remove scans of the remaining partitions for the recent 7-day filter. Gzip JSON is row-based, so queries read all columns, and gzip is also disadvantageous for split reads. Parquet without partitions saves on columns but targets the files of every date. Partitioning by user ID does not match the query pattern and degrades performance through small files and an explosion of partitions.

prompt: A research company's analytics team runs a Spark job on Amazon EMR for 4 hours once a day. Because some intermediate results remain in HDFS, the job must not restart from the beginning even if nodes are lost, and the company wants to cut cost as much as possible. When the job finishes, the cluster is terminated and restarted as a new cluster the next day. Input and final results are all stored in Amazon S3, and extra processing capacity is needed during peak hours. The team understands the possibility of Spot interruptions and will not modify the code. The HDFS data kept on core nodes during the job consists of temporary shuffle files and intermediate tables. Which TWO configurations meet the requirements? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Run core nodes as Spot Instances and lower the HDFS replication factor to 1 to reduce storage cost, assuming node loss is acceptable.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Configure the primary and core nodes as On-Demand Instances to protect HDFS data and the cluster from being lost to Spot interruptions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Configure the primary, core, and task nodes all as Spot Instances to get the maximum possible discount, and resubmit the job if interrupted.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Configure only core nodes as large On-Demand Instances without task nodes so that peak throughput is always secured, and do not use Spot.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Secure the extra processing capacity by configuring task nodes as Spot Instances in an instance fleet that specifies several instance types.

explanation: The correct answers are keeping the primary and core nodes On-Demand and configuring the task nodes as a Spot Instance fleet with diverse instance types. Core nodes store data in HDFS, so data can be lost if they are terminated, and the cluster ends if the primary is terminated. Task nodes do not store data, so the impact of Spot interruptions is small, which makes them suitable for capacity expansion. All-Spot would require restarts because of lost intermediate results and violates the requirement. Running core nodes on Spot while lowering the replication factor actually increases the risk of HDFS loss. Using only large On-Demand core nodes increases cost unnecessarily.

prompt: A team at a SaaS company wants to enable the UltraWarm tier on an Amazon OpenSearch Service domain. The domain currently uses 3 data nodes with t3.medium.search instances and has no dedicated master nodes. The goal is to reduce log retention cost, and the domain spans 3 Availability Zones. When the team tries to add warm nodes in the console, it reports that the domain does not meet the prerequisites. The team wants to resolve this by changing the existing domain configuration without creating a new domain. Logs accumulate in daily indexes, and the indexes to be moved to the warm tier are old indexes that are no longer written to. Which TWO conditions must be met to enable UltraWarm? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enable dedicated master nodes on the domain.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create the S3 bucket in which warm data will be stored yourself and link the bucket name in the domain settings.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Turn off encryption at rest on the domain so that warm nodes can read unencrypted objects in S3.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Change the data nodes to an instance type other than T2 or T3.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduce the number of replicas of all indexes in the domain to 0 so that no replicas remain when moving to the warm tier.

explanation: The correct answers are enabling dedicated master nodes and using a data node type other than T2 or T3. The official documentation states that to use warm storage, the domain must have dedicated master nodes, and that warm storage cannot be used if data nodes are T2 or T3 instance types. Reducing the number of replicas to 0 is not a requirement, and replicas of warm indexes are passive replicas that do not use disk. The S3 storage is managed by the service, so you do not create and link a bucket yourself. Turning off encryption is not a condition and is unrelated to the warm tier.

prompt: A marketing analytics team uses an Amazon Redshift Serverless workgroup, and inefficient analyst queries once caused month-end cost to exceed the budget. Some reduction in query performance is acceptable, but monthly cost must not exceed a ceiling, and the human intervention needed to manage this must be minimal. The workgroup is shared by 30 analysts and has a base capacity of 128 RPUs. The organization will not accept turning queries themselves into an approval process. Budget approval is made monthly, and an approach of only receiving cost-overrun alerts was already tried before without effect. Which configuration MOST appropriately meets this requirement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Set the Max RPU-hours usage limit and the maximum capacity (Max capacity) on the workgroup so that the service scales and consumes only within these limits.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Raise the base capacity to 512 RPUs so that queries always finish quickly with ample resources and the time consumed is reduced.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Move the price-performance target slider toward performance optimization so that even inefficient queries scale aggressively and finish quickly.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Set as an operating guideline that an owner manually pauses the workgroup after the 20th of each month and restarts it at the start of the month.

explanation: Setting the Max RPU-hours and maximum capacity limits is the correct answer. The documentation explains that Max capacity and Max RPU-hours limit the maximum RPUs that serverless can scale to and the maximum RPU-hours it can consume, and that they are always honored and enforced regardless of the price-performance target. This keeps the monthly ceiling without human intervention, and it matches the stated tolerance for lower performance. Raising the base capacity increases the RPU rate and usage, so cost actually grows. The performance-optimized target scales aggressively even if it costs more. Manual pausing involves a lot of human intervention and blocks month-end work.

prompt: A mobility company has an Apache Iceberg table that it queries with Athena. Streaming ingestion creates tens of thousands of small Parquet files per day, and delete files from row-level DELETE operations also accumulate, so queries are getting slower. Old snapshots and orphan files keep increasing Amazon S3 storage and metadata. The table is registered in the AWS Glue Data Catalog, and time travel to snapshots within the last 7 days must be maintained. Most queries read recent partitions, and DELETE operations occur mainly because of personal data deletion requests. Which TWO methods solve these two problems in Athena without operating a new cluster? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Run MSCK REPAIR TABLE regularly to re-register partitions, assuming that small files are merged automatically and delete files are applied to data files, and schedule it to run every night.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Apply a lifecycle rule to the S3 bucket that deletes all objects older than 30 days after creation so that old snapshots and orphan files are removed together, and include the files used by the current table in the same rule.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Run an OPTIMIZE ... REWRITE DATA USING BIN_PACK statement to merge small data files and delete files into files closer to the target size and rewrite them.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Run an AWS Glue crawler every hour to reread the table schema, assuming that old snapshots in the Iceberg metadata are cleaned up when the crawler runs, and set the crawler schedule to hourly.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Specify a snapshot retention period in the table properties and then run a VACUUM statement to clean up expired snapshots and remove orphan files that do not belong to the current state.

explanation: OPTIMIZE and VACUUM are the correct answers. OPTIMIZE REWRITE DATA rewrites data files into a better layout based on file size and the number of associated delete files, which resolves the small file and delete file problems. VACUUM performs snapshot expiration and orphan file removal, deleting only items older than the retention period (vacuum_max_snapshot_age_seconds), which reduces metadata and storage. A crawler only reads schemas and partitions and neither cleans up snapshots nor merges files. MSCK REPAIR TABLE is a partition registration command and has no file merging effect. An S3 lifecycle deletion can also delete data files that the current table references, which could break the table.

prompt: About 30 nightly AWS Glue ETL jobs at a fintech data team occasionally fail or exceed their timeouts. When a failure or timeout occurs, a notification must be sent to an Amazon SNS topic connected to the operations channel without changing the job code. The company wants to avoid the operational burden of adding notification logic to each job. Currently, an owner checks the run history in the console by hand every morning, so automation is needed. Jobs will continue to be added, and the company does not want to create separate notification settings even when new jobs are created. The notification message must include the job name and the failure state, and the operations channel already subscribes to the SNS topic. Which configuration is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add a try/except block at the end of each AWS Glue job script and modify the code to call SNS Publish when an exception is caught. All scripts would have to be fixed and redeployed, and SNS publish permission would also have to be added to each job role.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create a metric filter that counts the ERROR string in each job's log group, and set up a CloudWatch alarm per job that fires when the value is 1 or greater.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In an Amazon EventBridge rule, match the FAILED and TIMEOUT states among Glue Job State Change events and specify the SNS topic as the target.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Configure an S3 event notification on the output S3 path so that a notification is sent if no new object is created by a specified time.

explanation: An EventBridge rule on Glue Job State Change is the correct answer. AWS Glue sends job state change events to EventBridge for SUCCEEDED, FAILED, TIMEOUT, and STOPPED, so matching the two states and sending them to SNS lets one rule monitor 30-plus jobs without changing job code. Exception handling inside scripts requires fixing all the code and does not run when a job is forcibly terminated due to a timeout. Log metric filters must be configured per job and cannot reliably catch TIMEOUT through log strings. S3 events occur only when an object is created, so they cannot detect that an object was not created.
